overview: Plateosaurus engelhardti was one of the most successful dinosaurs of the Late Triassic — a large prosauropod reaching up to seven metres, known from over 100 individuals across central Europe (Germany, France, Switzerland). It was a committed biped that could not walk on four legs, despite early reconstructions showing a quadrupedal posture, and its body plan presages the giant sauropods that would evolve from its lineage.

Mass-death sites in Germany and Switzerland — where dozens of individuals of all sizes are found together — suggest many individuals became mired in soft ground, possibly during seasonal migrations toward water in a semi-arid Triassic landscape. Bone texture studies show that Plateosaurus grew more like a reptile (variable growth rate) than like a bird or mammal (rapid determinate growth).

fossilSites.note: Late Triassic (Norian) fluvial sandstones with abundant Plateosaurus material including mass-death accumulations.

fossilSites.name: Knollenmergel Formation — Trossingen
fossilSites.note: Classic mass-death site with dozens of Plateosaurus individuals; excavated by Friedrich von Huene in the 1920s and 30s.

fossilSites.name: Frick site
fossilSites.note: Swiss Triassic beds with extensive Plateosaurus material currently under ongoing excavation.

articles.title: Discovery and abundance
articles.body: Friedrich von Huene described the genus in 1837, long before the dinosaur concept was formalised. Over 100 individuals are now known, making Plateosaurus one of the most abundant Triassic dinosaurs. The Trossingen quarry in Germany and the Frick site in Switzerland have produced dozens of articulated specimens.

articles.title: Locomotion debate
articles.body: For much of the 20th century Plateosaurus was reconstructed as a facultative quadruped. Detailed biomechanical analysis by Bonnan and Senter (2007) and others showed its wrist anatomy prevented pronation — the hand could not be placed flat on the ground for walking. Plateosaurus was an obligate biped, using its forelimbs only for grasping.

articles.title: Growth biology
articles.body: Bone histology of Plateosaurus samples shows variable growth rates between individuals of the same size — unlike the predictable rapid growth of birds and mammals. This "reptilian" growth strategy means that Plateosaurus individuals reached similar adult sizes at very different ages. The same feeding resources and climate produced very different growth trajectories, suggesting growth was strongly environmentally controlled rather than genetically fixed.

fossilRecord.material: Large numbers of skeletons from Germany and Switzerland.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Triassic European terrestrial basins with mass-death assemblages.
fossilRecord.evidence: Growth series and skeletons document a large bipedal sauropodomorph before true giant sauropods.

record.description: Plateosaurus was a large non-sauropodan sauropodomorph from Late Triassic Europe, represented by many skeletons and bonebed assemblages. Species-level nomenclature, especially P. engelhardti versus P. trossingensis, has a complex history.
facts: The Trossingen and Frick bonebeds preserve many individuals of different sizes.
Biomechanical work favours habitual bipedality for adults rather than elephant-like quadrupedal walking.
Size varied substantially among mature individuals, consistent with developmental plasticity.

presentation.heroLead: The best-known early sauropodomorph, dug from Central European bonebeds in such numbers that its skeleton, growth and posture are known in unusual detail.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Plateosaurus
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Plateosaurus in side view, walking bipedally with a long neck and small head
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by TotalDino. The bipedal posture follows biomechanical studies of complete skeletons; skin texture and colour are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Plateosaurus was a long-necked, small-headed plant-eater from the Late Triassic of Central Europe, one of the first large dinosaurs in the fossil record. Mature animals ranged from roughly five to ten metres long, a spread that bone histology attributes to individuals growing to very different final sizes rather than to several species.

Digital modelling of complete skeletons shows that its forelimbs could not be turned palm-down to bear weight, so adults walked on their hind legs; the large thumb claw and grasping hand were free for other uses. Leaf-shaped, coarsely serrated teeth indicate a plant diet, probably taken from shrubs and low trees.

The genus was named in 1837 from fragmentary bones near Nuremberg, but its fame rests on the mass graves at Trossingen and Halberstadt in Germany and Frick in Switzerland, where dozens of animals apparently became mired in mud. The species names have a tangled history, settled in 2019 when P. trossingensis and its complete Stuttgart skeleton were fixed as the reference for the genus.
animalHighlights: Dozens of skeletons from bonebeds document every part of the body, from skull to tail tip.
Adults of the same age reached very different sizes, a rare direct record of developmental plasticity in a dinosaur.
Forelimb anatomy rules out weight-bearing on the hands, supporting habitual bipedality.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Serrated leaf-shaped teeth and a downturned jaw joint fit cropping vegetation; gastroliths once claimed are not confirmed.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The hands could not pronate to take weight, so adults moved on two legs; trackways are not securely attributed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Many complete skeletons give reliable lengths; mass estimates of roughly 600 to 4,000 kilograms depend on the individual and method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions are secure from complete skeletons; skin, colour and any soft-tissue outline are not preserved.

whereFacts.label: Rock unit
whereFacts.value: Trossingen, Löwenstein and equivalent Keuper units

locality.name: Trossingen bonebed
locality.note: The best-sampled site, worked in 1911–1912, 1921–1923 and 1932. The original 1834 find came from Heroldsberg near Nuremberg; other major bonebeds are Halberstadt in Germany and Frick in Switzerland.

presentation.classificationSummary: Plateosaurus is the name-bearing genus of Plateosauridae, a group of Late Triassic sauropodomorphs outside Sauropoda. It is the reference taxon for early sauropodomorph anatomy. Since 2019 P. trossingensis has been the type species, with P. engelhardti and P. gracilis also recognised by many workers.

related.reason: A smaller, later sauropodomorph from southern Africa known from a comparable growth series.
A heavier-bodied Late Triassic sauropodomorph from Argentina for comparison of posture.
A Chinese Early Jurassic plateosaur-like form once placed in the same family.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: P. trossingensis, P. engelhardti and P. gracilis are the main names in use, but the fragmentary Heroldsberg type material makes some assignments hard to test.

questions.title: Why do adults differ so much in size?
questions.copy: Histology shows animals of similar age stopping growth at very different sizes. Whether environment, sex or something else drove this is unknown.

questions.title: How did the bonebeds form?
questions.copy: Animals trapped in mud, seasonal drought and flood transport have all been proposed for Trossingen and Frick; the mud-trap model best explains the upright, partly articulated skeletons.

review.ageReviewNote: Well-dated occurrences span Norian-Rhaetian European strata; species-level horizons should be retained separately.

specimens.name: Lectotype of P. engelhardti
specimens.note: Fragmentary postcranial bones found in 1834 at Heroldsberg near Nuremberg and named by von Meyer in 1837, the first sauropodomorph and one of the earliest dinosaurs described.

specimens.name: Holotype of P. trossingensis
specimens.note: A nearly complete articulated skeleton from Trossingen described by Fraas in 1913; fixed by the ICZN in 2019 as the name-bearing type of the type species.

specimens.name: Tübingen skeleton 1
specimens.note: A nearly complete individual from Trossingen used for digital reconstruction and biomechanical modelling of posture and gait.

panel.headline: Dozens of skeletons from Triassic mass graves.
panel.standfirst: Plateosaurus is known from more than a hundred individuals, many of them articulated and nearly complete, recovered from bonebeds at Trossingen, Halberstadt and Frick. It is the most completely documented dinosaur of the Triassic.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every region of the skeleton is represented by multiple articulated individuals, including complete skulls, hands, feet and tails, across a range of body sizes.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with teeth, full vertebral series, ribs and gastralia, shoulder and hip girdles, forelimbs with the enlarged thumb claw, hindlimbs and feet, from many articulated skeletons of different sizes.
knownRemains.note: The abundance is concentrated in a few bonebeds, so the genus is exceptionally well known anatomically while the original Heroldsberg type material remains too fragmentary to compare closely.

media.title: Skeleton GPIT/RE/7288 at the University of Tübingen
media.alt: Mounted skeleton of Plateosaurus, specimen GPIT/RE/7288, at the University of Tübingen
media.caption: A nearly complete individual from the Trossingen bonebed, one of the skeletons digitised for biomechanical study. Mounted in the bipedal posture supported by limb anatomy.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls with dentition and braincases from Trossingen, Halberstadt and Frick.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in articulated skeletons, with ribs, gastralia and chevrons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete girdles, forelimbs with hands and thumb claws, hindlimbs and feet from numerous individuals.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bone histology across many individuals records growth; no skin, colour or confirmed gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: SMNS 13200 · holotype of P. trossingensis
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete articulated skeleton excavated at Trossingen and described by Eberhard Fraas in 1913. In 2019 the ICZN made P. trossingensis the type species of the genus, anchoring the name to this well-preserved specimen.
specimenCards.meta: Trossingen, Germany · Trossingen Formation · Staatliches Museum für Naturkunde Stuttgart

specimenCards.title: UEN 552 · lectotype of P. engelhardti
specimenCards.description: Fragmentary bones found in 1834 by Johann Friedrich Engelhardt at Heroldsberg and named by Hermann von Meyer in 1837. Their poor preservation is why the type species was later transferred to the Trossingen skeleton.
specimenCards.meta: Heroldsberg, Bavaria · Feuerletten · University of Erlangen-Nürnberg

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Complete articulated skeletons of many individuals of different sizes, with skulls, teeth, hands, feet and tails, from several bonebeds in Germany and Switzerland.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A habitually bipedal, browsing herbivore whose adults reached very different final sizes; bonebeds are read as animals trapped in mud rather than herds dying together.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: How many species the material represents, the cause of size variation, the animal's exact posture at rest, and any soft-tissue or colour detail.
